summary: A technical deep dive focused on aligning quantization strategies (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) with Aperture Financial's latency SLOs and throughput targets. Discussed orchestration decisions: per-route precision gating, KV cache warmstart, batching policies, and deterministic fallback to higher-precision models in VPC/on-prem contexts. Team agreed to run a workload-driven benchmark and exchange golden prompts for regression checks.
topics: Precision gating by route and user tier
Batch sizing and latency SLO trade-offs
Quantization regressions: GPTQ vs AWQ vs INT8
VPC/on-prem deployment constraints and KMS integration
transcript:
[00:00] Lina Ortiz: okay everyone, thanks for joining, um we're on the call to go through the SLO-driven quantization approach. We have aperture's infra and ml folks, hi everyone.
[00:10] Raj Patel: hey hi, thanks. audio's good. we've been seeing a couple of post-quantize accuracy blips in prod-like tests, and some latency wins but also tail spikes when kvcache misses.
[00:25] Marcus Chen: right, and to be clear, we're not just swapping one quant method for another, we're talking about per-route precision orchestration — like, keep conversation routes at fp16, batch-summarization at int8, or mix with gptq.
[00:38] Sofia Martinez: quick context — production workload is ~12k QPS at peak across many short-turn chats, typical token sequence 16-80, 75% of requests are conversational. Our SLO is p99 latency 250ms for the high-priority tier.
[00:55] Priya Rao: got it. also we heard aperture wants private deployment options (VPC and potential on-prem) for regulated data, so we need to consider how quantization tooling and fallback works without our hosted assist.
[01:10] Tom Whitaker: yes security: KMS integration and audit logs are mandatory. we can't have model weights leaving our VPC.
[01:18] Lina Ortiz: noted — we'll attach SOC2 docs and a KMS integration guide after the call. but today let's focus on runtime-level choices: int8/awq/gptq/fp8 tradeoffs, kv warmstart strategies, batching policies, and how fallbacks trigger.
[01:35] Raj Patel: ok first question — what's the observed accuracy delta between gptq and awq on say, instruction/LLM style prompts? we've seen more hallucinations in awq configs before.
[01:45] Marcus Chen: good question. short answer: it depends on model and calibration. in our lab tests with a 7B style model, gptq tends to preserve logits ordering better for classification tasks, awq often compresses distribution tails which can change beam scoring and cause phrasing regressions. but AWQ gets better perf and smaller memory.
[02:05] Sofia Martinez: when you say "preserve logits ordering" is that a deterministic guarantee?
[02:10] Marcus Chen: not a guarantee, but empirical. GPTQ uses per-channel quant with a reconstruction pass which often keeps relative token scores closer to fp16. AWQ is faster and uses different per-tensor block algos so you see shifts in low-prob tokens.
[02:25] Raj Patel: and INT8? we ran an int8 pipeline with hybrid FP16 for attention and saw smaller mem but bad tails for multi-step prompts.
[02:35] Priya Rao: that's expected. INT8 without careful layer-wise calibration or mixed-precision—like keeping softmax and layernorm at fp16—will blow up multi-step coherence.
[02:45] Marcus Chen: exactly. one of the patterns we recommend: precision gating. keep KV cache and attention matmuls quantized but keep layernorm/softmax at higher precision and force fp16 for last n layers in sensitive routes.
[02:58] Tom Whitaker: how do we control that in the private runtime? can we set per-route profiles?
[03:05] Marcus Chen: yes, Redwood Private supports per-route model variant mapping and a precision profile. You can define policy: route.name=="financial-advice" -> model=apx-7b-gptq, precision_gating={last_k_layers: 4, layernorm: fp16}.
[03:20] Sofia Martinez: policy language looks good, but what about KV cache warmstart — our issue is cold cache tails where first user requests hit high latency.
[03:28] Marcus Chen: two approaches: proactive warmstart via prefix caching pre-populated with common tokens or user-session sticky warm caches. For heavy chat workloads we push a shadow warmup traffic that prefetches KV states for active sessions at low priority. That's what reduced p99 by ~20% in our internal benchmarks.
[03:43] Raj Patel: shadow warmup sounds expensive, especially if it doubles token costs.
[03:48] Priya Rao: it's workload-aware — you define a warmup budget and a TTL for warm entries. For sessions with high churn we use shorter TTLs; for repeat sessions we keep sticky entries. It reduces tokens served because many requests then avoid recomputing early layers.
[04:00] Sofia Martinez: curious — do quantized KV caches change cache hit semantics? like, if kv stored in INT8 vs FP16, does it affect mismatch when switching precision on fallback?
[04:09] Marcus Chen: good observation. yes you can get mismatches if you store an INT8 representation and then serve a fallback fp16 model because the kv tensors are not bit-for-bit compatible. We handle this by versioning the KV cache entries with a precision tag and performing automatic re-warm if there's a mismatch. That re-warm is the tail spike you saw.
[04:28] Tom Whitaker: so the fallback path is expensive — how do you avoid cascading failures?
[04:33] Marcus Chen: policy-based fallbacks: we prefer per-request local fallback that recomputes a small prefix at fp16 just to get a stable KV state rather than a full recompute. Also we limit concurrent fallbacks using a circuit-breaker so the system doesn't thundering herd onto the fp16 pool.
[04:50] Raj Patel: could you explain "recompute a small prefix"? if a 20-token prefix is recomputed at fp16, do we merge it into the INT8 cache?
[04:58] Marcus Chen: yes, we recompute the last N tokens at the higher precision and then quantize+store them if necessary, or keep a separate fp16 sticky slot for that session depending on memory. This reduces the amount of data to recompute vs full conversation rewind.
[05:12] Sofia Martinez: what about determinism for audits? For financial use we need deterministic outputs for given prompts during investigations. Quantization-induced nondeterminism is a compliance problem.
[05:22] Maya Li: exactly — we need explainability and reproducible outputs for at least a month worth of critical transactions.
[05:28] Priya Rao: we support deterministic inference modes — pin random seeds and use stable kernels — but quantization can still change model logits. For auditability we recommend: keep golden-verification mode at fp16 for compliance-critical routes and store golden outputs in a ledger. Also have a canary A/B path that replays a sample at fp16 to detect regressions.
[05:48] Raj Patel: how expensive is that replay?
[05:50] Marcus Chen: depends on sampling rate. For a 1% sample it’s usually a small cost compared to total. We also offer off-peak replay scheduling.
[05:58] Tom Whitaker: back to AWQ vs GPTQ — we want to test with our actual prompts. what's the plan?
[06:05] Lina Ortiz: Marcus will run a batch of Aperture's prompts through the three presets — INT8-hybrid, GPTQ, AWQ — with KV warm/cold scenarios. We'll produce comparative metrics: p50/p95/p99, token cost delta, and an accuracy score using Sofia's golden outputs.
[06:20] Sofia Martinez: I'll upload a 500 prompt set with 50 golden outputs and a scoring rubric; we prefer BLEU+embedding-sim and manual categories for hallucination.
[06:29] Marcus Chen: perfect. I'll include layerwise sensitivity logs too — the runtime can produce per-layer KL divergence between fp16 and quantized activations so we can pinpoint sensitive layers.
[06:40] Raj Patel: is the layerwise KL heavy to compute online?
[06:44] Marcus Chen: we run it offline during the benchmarking phase. For production we provide a lightweight probe that samples a tiny set.
[06:50] Sofia Martinez: another constraint — our on-prem GPUs are mixed (A100s and some 80GB H100s); will the runtime pick kernels appropriately?
[06:59] Priya Rao: yes, runtime kernel selection is per-host. It picks optimized kernels per architecture and quant format. We also offer a heterogenous pool routing policy so heavy-precision workloads go to H100s and quantized paths to A100s.
[07:15] Tom Whitaker: routing across pool types — how do we manage model variant compatibility? e.g., gptq weights on H100 and awq on A100.
[07:23] Marcus Chen: models are compiled per-variant+hardware combo and we keep an index of compatible fallbacks. The router will only send requests to compatible hosts; if capacity isn't available, it will either queue or fallback to the hosted variant based on your policy.
[07:36] Raj Patel: queueing is risky for us. we prefer graceful degradation on quality (shorter responses) vs increased latency.
[07:44] Lina Ortiz: you can set a policy: prefer degrade-quality -> reduce max tokens and lower beam width before escalating to increased latency or switching to a higher-cost fp16 route. We call this quality-first or latency-first modes.
[07:59] Sofia Martinez: can we do per-customer SLOs? for our enterprise customers we need different p99 targets.
[08:06] Marcus Chen: yes, per-customer and per-route SLOs are supported. The optimizer will pick batching and quant profiles to satisfy SLOs while minimizing cost.
[08:16] Raj Patel: speaking of batching, do larger batches help quantized runtimes? we saw increased throughput but tail latency went up.
[08:23] Marcus Chen: continuous batching helps amortize kernel launch costs and improves token throughput, but for chat-style low-latency requests we use a small max batch and dynamic batching. The key is predicting seq length distribution; Redwood's batcher uses a time/size hybrid.
[08:36] Tom Whitaker: how does KV cache affect batchability? if different sessions have different prefixes lengths, batching gets weird.
[08:42] Marcus Chen: we shard batches by comparable sequence lengths and by whether the request is cache-hit vs miss. Cache-hit requests are cheap and can piggyback in the same batch; cache-miss requests often trigger extra compute so we isolate them to avoid stragglers.
[08:55] Sofia Martinez: any recommendations for our threshold config? we have lots of short chats (<40 tokens).
[09:00] Marcus Chen: for your distribution we suggest max batch 16, max latency wait 10ms for high-priority tier, and aggressive sticky KV for returning sessions. For background jobs (summarization) max batch 64 with 50ms wait. These are starting suggestions; Marcus will run and tune.
[09:15] Raj Patel: question on metrics — how do we surface quantization regressions over time? we need alerts when semantic similarity drops for a cohort.
[09:23] Marcus Chen: Redwood Optimize integrates evals tied to prompt sets. You can set regression thresholds (e.g., embedding similarity delta > 0.03) and get alerts. We also surface per-route token-cost deltas and p99 shifts.
[09:36] Sofia Martinez: okay good. last: can we do a phased rollout? start with 10% of traffic to INT8-hybrid then increase to 50% if no regressions.
[09:44] Lina Ortiz: yes canary rollouts are supported by percentage and by user cohort. We also do automatic rollback on regression alerts.
[09:53] Raj Patel: nice. any gotchas for on-prem licensing or offline upgrades?
[09:57] Priya Rao: for on-prem we ship a private control plane image and a runtime agent; model artifacts stay within your infra. Upgrades require a maintenance window for kernel/driver compatibility checks — we'll coordinate.
[10:10] Tom Whitaker: fine. let's confirm timeline then.
[10:13] Lina Ortiz: action items recap — Marcus runs benchmarks; Sofia provides prompts; Tom confirms access; Lina sends security docs. we'll reconvene after the benchmark results.
[10:25] Sofia Martinez: thanks all.
[10:27] Raj Patel: thanks.
[10:29] Marcus Chen: thanks folks, we'll follow up in the tracker.
[10:33] [meeting ended]
